text:
alice: Heads-up — during last night's soak we saw a bunch of PodPending spikes in eu-west-1 when spot pools got preempted. Thinking through Karpenter handling for spot saturation + ENI limits. Anyone seen similar?

ben: saw that too. metrics: 60% of GPU workloads hit Pending within a 7m window after AZ spot reclaim. ENI errors in node events.

chandra: can you paste the event logs? we need to know if it's kube-scheduler waiting or ENI allocation failing at instance boot.

alice: logs: 
```
Normal  Scheduled  Pod default/foo  Successfully assigned default/foo to ip-192-168-10-45.eu-west-1.compute.internal
Warning  FailedCreatePodSandBox  Pod default/bar  failed to set up sandbox container: rpc error: code = Unknown desc = failed to allocate pod IP: "failed to allocate address: ENI subnet ip exhaustion"
```

marta: ouch. that looks like ENI capacity per instance type + trunking hitting account limits, not just Karpenter. we have high fragmentation across 3 provs.

ben: summary from metrics + costs: we were using 4 separate provisioners (gpu-spot-1, gpu-spot-2, gpu-on-demand, general-gpu). fragmentation causes small leftover IP pools per AZ. warm-pool would help but costs.

chandra: two related problems: 1) spot reclaim => burst of new pods; 2) new nodes can't attach ENIs fast enough (AWS quota or trunking limit). Karpenter keeps spinning up instances but they fail networking, keep retrying => spin loops and extra cost.

alice: proposed mitigations: 
- single consolidated GPU provisioner per region with instanceTypes list to reduce fragmentation
- configure TTLSecondsUntilExpired and consolidationThreshold to reclaim idle nodes quicker
- fallback policy: prefer spot, but allow on-demand when ENI errors or scaled failure rate > 5%
- enable a tiny warm pool (1-2 nodes) in each AZ for critical queues

marta: +1. also we should add an admission hook to mark batch pods with lower nic limits? (not ideal). alternatively throttle parallel pod creation when node pool capacity is below threshold.

ben: example Karpenter provisioner snippet I tested: 
```
apiVersion: karpenter.sh/v1alpha5
kind: Provisioner
metadata:
  name: gpu-consol-eu-west
spec:
  requirements:
    - key: "karpenter.k8s.aws/capacity-type"
      operator: In
      values: ["spot", "on-demand"]
  provider:
    subnetSelector:
      karpenter.sh/discovery: "eu-west-1"
  ttlSecondsUntilExpired: 3600
  consolidation:
    enabled: true
```
This reduced fragmentation in my run.

chandra: how do we detect ENI exhaustion to switch capacity-type automatically? we could build a simple controller watching node events and annotate provisioner to prefer on-demand, or use the webhook in the control plane to prefer fallback.

alice: idea: Karpenter has Leases/Events we can read. devops-bot could emit an alert when >N ENI allocation failures in 5m, trigger a runbook to flip provisioner selector or create short-lived on-demand pool. Would that be acceptable ops-wise?

devops-bot: alert rule suggestion: 
- name: karpenter_aws_eni_failures_high
- expr: increase(karpenter_node_event_count{reason="FailedCreatePodSandBox",region="eu-west-1"}[5m]) > 3
- action: create incident + call /runbooks/eni-fallback

marta: runbook should include steps: bump on-demand percentage, wait 10m, watch for pending count drop, then scale back. also check Account ENI quotas and request limit raise.

ben: cost question: if we flip 20% to on-demand during floods, what's the monthly hit? rough guesstimate: +12% on GPU bill for eu-west workloads at current run rates. cheaper than repeated cold starts and wasted retries.

chandra: agree. also consider smarter bin-packing: prefer instance types with higher pod density (more IPs) during high-concurrency batch windows. that reduces ENI pressure.

alice: follow-ups: 
- chandra/marta to prototype small controller that watches node events -> annotates provisioner (or posts to SRE webhook)
- ben to run cost sim for 10/20/50% fallback on-demand for a month
- infra to open support ticket for ENI quota review with AWS for target AZs

marta: I'll draft a 1-page decision doc and a short playbook for the on-call run.

chandra: I'll prototype controller this week. if we can automate to only flip when pending > X and ENI errors > Y, we can keep warm pools minimal.

alice: perfect. thanks all. tagging @oncall for visibility. :pray: 

devops-bot: Incident created: INC-2026-0456 (auto) — karpenter_aws_eni_failures_high — assigned to eng-infra oncall.
